definitions.text: We know that the set of rational numbers is defined as Q = {p/q; p, q ∈ Z ∧ q ≠ 0}
and set of irrational numbers (Q') contains those elements which cannot be expressed as quotient of integers.
The set of Real numbers is the union of the set of rational numbers and irrational numbers i,e., R = Q ∪ Q'
A decimal number with a finite number of digits after the decimal point is called a terminating decimal number.
The decimal numbers with an infinitely repeating pattern of digits after the decimal point are called non-terminating and recurring decimal numbers.
Non-terminating and non-recurring decimal numbers are known as irrational numbers.
a + b ∈ R
a + b = b + a
a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c
ab ∈ R
ab = ba
a(bc) = (ab)c

definitions.term: Left distributive property of multiplication over addition
definitions.text:
For all real numbers a, b, c

(i) a(b + c) = ab + ac is called left distributive property of multiplication over addition.
∀ a ∈ R, a = a
∀ a,b ∈ R, a = b ⇒ b = a
∀ a,b,c ∈ R, a = b ∧ b = c ⇒ a = c
∀ a,b,c ∈ R, a = b ⇒ a + c = b + c
∀ a,b,c ∈ R, a = b ⇒ ac = bc
∀ a,b,c ∈ R, a + c = b + c ⇒ a = b
∀ a,b,c ∈ R and c ≠ 0, ac = bc ⇒ a = b
∀ a,b ∈ R, either a = b or a > b or a < b
If n is a positive integer greater than 1 and a is a real number, then any real number x such that x = ⁿ√a is called nᵗʰ root of a.
Here, √ is called radical and n is the index of radical. A real number under the radical sign is called a radicand.
Exponential form of x = ⁿ√a is x = (a)^(1/n).
An irrational radical with rational radicand is called a surd.
A surd that contains a single term is called a monomial surd e.g., √5, √7 etc.
A surd that contains the sum of two monomial surds is called a binomial surd e.g., √3 + √5, √2 + √7 etc.
√a + √b and √a − √b are called conjugate surds of each other.
The product of two conjugate surds is a rational number.
To rationalize a denominator of the form a + b√x or a − b√x, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate factor.

fullMarks: For a rational-or-irrational question, state the reason as well as the answer: terminating or recurring decimals are rational; non-terminating, non-recurring decimals are irrational.
When converting a recurring decimal to p/q, define x, multiply by 10, 100, or the needed power of 10, subtract to cancel the recurring digits, and finish by writing the fraction.
For a number-line construction, show the right triangle and its labelled lengths, use the Pythagoras step to obtain the required root, then mark and label the point on the number line.
When naming a property, give its full name carefully: distinguish commutative from associative, and identify whether a property is for equality or order.
For rationalization, multiply both numerator and denominator by the conjugate, show the denominator becoming a difference of squares, and simplify the final result.
For indices and radicals, first rewrite numbers with a common base or as fractional powers; show each index-law step before simplifying.
In a proof or verification, calculate the LHS and RHS separately, show that they are equal, and end with a clear statement that the property is verified.
mistakes: Calling a decimal irrational just because it has many digits. Fix: check whether it terminates or has a repeating pattern; only non-terminating, non-recurring decimals are irrational.
Treating every irrational number as a surd. Fix: a surd must be an irrational radical with a rational radicand; √π is not a surd.
Confusing the commutative property with the associative property. Fix: commutative changes order; associative changes grouping with brackets.
Forgetting to reverse an inequality after multiplying or dividing by a negative number. Fix: reverse < to >, or > to <, whenever the multiplier or divisor is negative.
Using the same surd instead of its conjugate when rationalizing. Fix: change the sign between the two terms, then multiply top and bottom by that conjugate.
Applying index laws to unlike bases without first rewriting them. Fix: express the terms using a common base before combining powers.
Giving only a point for a number-line question without showing the construction. Fix: draw and label the triangle or fraction divisions, mark the point, and name the value.
